sources.citation: Harlow, J. M. (1848). Passage of an Iron Rod through the Head. The Boston Medical and Surgical Journal, 39(20), 389-393.
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref (10.1056/NEJM184812130392001) and Wikisource full text. Reports the September 13, 1848 blast in Cavendish, Vermont, the 3 ft 7 in, 13.25 lb tamping iron, Gage riding upright 3/4 mile in an ox cart, walking up stairs at Joseph Adams's hotel, and his acute clinical course through November 1848.

sources.citation: Harlow, J. M. (1868). Recovery from the passage of an iron bar through the head. Publications of the Massachusetts Medical Society, 2, 327-347 (reprinted in History of Psychiatry, 1993, 4(14), 274-281).
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref (10.1177/0957154X9300401407) and Wikisource full text. Gives the classic post-injury behavioral description ('fitful, irreverent... no longer Gage'), contractors refusing to reinstate him as foreman, his livery work in Hanover, stagecoach driving of six-horse teams between Valparaiso and Santiago in Chile, his epileptic seizures in San Francisco, and exhumation of his skull.

sources.citation: Bigelow, H. J. (1850). Dr. Harlow's Case of Recovery from the passage of an Iron Bar through the Head. The American Journal of the Medical Sciences, 20, 13-22.
sources.notes: Verified archival full text on Wikisource. Harvard surgery professor Henry Jacob Bigelow examined Gage in Boston in 1850, commissioned the plaster life cast of his head, and demonstrated the iron's trajectory on a prepared skull.

sources.citation: Damasio, H., Grabowski, T., Frank, R., Galaburda, A. M., & Damasio, A. R. (1994). The Return of Phineas Gage: Clues About the Brain from the Skull of a Famous Patient. Science, 264(5162), 1102-1105.
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref and PubMed (PMID 8178168). First modern 3D computer reconstruction based on skull measurements deformed onto a standard skull; argued that damage hit both left and right ventromedial prefrontal cortices while sparing Broca's and motor cortex.

sources.citation: Ratiu, P., Talos, I.-F., Haker, S., Lieberman, D., & Everett, P. (2004). The Tale of Phineas Gage, Digitally Remastered. Journal of Neurotrauma, 21(5), 637-643 (also New England Journal of Medicine, 351(23), e21).
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref (10.1089/089771504774129964 and 10.1056/NEJMicm031024) and PubMed (PMID 15165371). Used thin-slice CT scans of Gage's actual skull from the Warren Museum and showed the lesion was strictly limited to the left frontal lobe, without crossing the midline or hitting the superior sagittal sinus.

sources.citation: Van Horn, J. D., Irimia, A., Torgerson, C. M., Chambers, M. C., Kikinis, R., & Toga, A. W. (2012). Mapping Connectivity Damage in the Case of Phineas Gage. PLoS ONE, 7(5), e37454.
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref and PubMed Central (PMC3353935). Combined the Warren Museum CT of Gage's skull with diffusion MRI connectomes of 110 right-handed males aged 25-36. Estimated ~4% (3.97%) cortical gray matter loss in the left frontal lobe (left orbital sulcus ~91%, orbital gyrus ~39%) and ~11% total white matter loss, severing uncinate fasciculus fibers between left orbitofrontal/ventromedial cortex and the amygdala/limbic system.

sources.citation: Warren Anatomical Museum, Center for the History of Medicine, Francis A. Countway Library of Medicine, Harvard Medical School. Phineas Gage Skull, Life Cast, and Tamping Iron Collection.
sources.notes: Verified Harvard Countway Library museum page and curator Dominic Hall's video presentation. Houses the original exhumed skull, the 110 cm (3 ft 7 in), 3.2 cm diameter engraved tamping iron, and Bigelow's 1850 plaster life mask.

sources.citation: Macmillan, M. (2002). Phineas Gage. In Encyclopedia of the Human Brain (and An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage, MIT Press, 2000).
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref (10.1016/b0-12-227210-2/00281-8 and 10.1016/b978-0-12-385157-4.00811-3). Documents how textbook accounts inflated Harlow's brief 1868 notes into a myth of a permanent violent psychopath, and corrects the death date to May 21, 1860 from San Francisco burial records.

sources.citation: Wilgus, J., & Wilgus, B. (2009). Face to Face with Phineas Gage. Journal of the History of the Neurosciences, 18(3), 340-345.
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref and PubMed (PMID 20183215). Authenticated the first known c. 1850 daguerreotype portrait of a well-dressed Phineas Gage with a closed left eyelid holding his inscribed tamping iron, matched against the Warren Museum life mask and iron.

sources.citation: Macmillan, M., & Lena, M. L. (2010). Rehabilitating Phineas Gage. Neuropsychological Rehabilitation, 20(5), 641-658.
sources.notes: Verified via Crossref (10.1080/09602011003760527). Presents historical eyewitness testimony from Chile (including an American physician in Valparaiso c. 1858-1859 who found 'no impairment whatever of his mental faculties') and argues that the structured daily routine of driving a six-horse stagecoach acted as social rehabilitation.
